Which module starts the first early pulse?

Each bar counts events. A module gets the event when it leads the other timed modules by more than 16 ns. If several modules start within 16 ns, the event goes into “Tied”. Each event is counted once.

This covers the first selected sharp pulse earlier than −100 µs, relative to the main shake. The bars summarise events and stay fixed while the maps play.

M6 does not lead alone in every measured event. In APA2 it leads alone in 38 of the 457 events where it can be timed, and shares the lead in 195. In APA1 the counts are 0 alone and 6 shared, from 12 events.

A “first” result compares the modules we could time. Missing recording cannot tell us whether another module started earlier. M8* in APA2 remains included as a disconnected electrical readout.

How was the start measured?

For each input, use the first sustained crossing of 20% of its downward pulse depth, or a noise threshold if larger. The existing calculation requires a quiet recorded baseline and three samples above threshold. Samples are 16 ns apart.

At least two inputs must have usable timings in a module. Its start is the earlier input time. Compare an event only if at least four modules qualify. The same input set is used for the 20% and 50% checks.

These checks show how often the earliest modules remain tied. The full-coverage check keeps events with all ten modules timed. The second-input check uses the later of the first two input starts in each module.

Where are the field cage and beam?

The field cage is on the right of the APA2 map above. The source slide uses a mirrored photograph to match that map. The AFE panel groups electronics, so its positions do not describe the detector.

These views show detector context. We still need a dimensioned drawing tied to the module map to place the beam axis, laser opening or support beams precisely.

Check the map orientation and sources

The field-cage label follows slide 18, including its channel order. Its photograph is explicitly flipped left to right to match the plots. The pictures above retain their source orientation; they have not been registered to one common coordinate frame.

EDMS 3493627 revision 1 is an archived working presentation, dated 21 July 2026. The beam overview is a dated conference presentation from 4 September 2025. Neither establishes surveyed module coordinates or a ground-shake source location.

Source files, pages and checksums

What do these maps measure?

Every input needs a complete 0.512 µs piece with no flagged rail code. An event needs at least twelve recorded inputs and four modules with at least two inputs each. Each cell then takes the middle value for that channel across those events. Disconnected inputs follow the same recording rules; they are not removed.

The colour can be relative to the largest channel response in each APA, or use one shared scale at the displayed time. The numbers stay in ADC counts. Neither view is a calibrated light measurement. The shared colour scale updates with time.

The two early-pulse buttons align each event to its selected pulse peak and show signal size. They are separate stage comparisons; their pulse times relative to the main shake differ between events. Play returns to the main-shake clock.

The contributing events change with time. A changing population map alone cannot establish movement within an event. The earlier slow-precursor summary uses module medians over a wider interval with sharp pulses removed.

Is there a correlation between AFEs?

Yes, during the main shake. Different AFEs share a strong waveform component. Signals on the same AFE usually match more closely.

These values measure correlation strength: 1 means matching shapes, including an inverted shape; 0 means no linear match. We compare four inputs at the same recorded times: two from different modules on each AFE. The counts are events with enough such comparisons.

These calculations include the recorded inputs of disconnected APA2 M8, on AFE 1. A shared waveform does not by itself prove crosstalk or locate the source. AFE grouping also overlaps detector position.

The matrix uses all eligible input pairs and therefore has different event counts from the four-input check above. Each square shows signed correlation and its event count. These are within-board comparisons; the boards were recorded in different runs.
